description: Hi! We are Team Maharashtra from the Pune local event, working on the "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge. We are passionate about using AI, machine learning, hardware, and Earth science data to solve real-world agricultural and weather problems. We are looking for enthusiastic teammates skilled in coding, data analysis, agriculture, or presentation/design. Join us to build an impactful solution together!
summary:
The "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data" challenge is a core problem statement from the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge. As global temperatures, rainfall patterns, and water availability shift, farmers need better ways to make informed decisions about what and when to plant.
The objective of this challenge is to create accessible, data-driven decision-support tools—such as interactive maps, visualizations, or predictive simulation models—that translate complex scientific information into actionable agricultural guidance. Participants are tasked with integrating public NASA Earth observations (like soil moisture, surface temperature, evaporation, and vegetation greenness) alongside local soil metrics, crop traits, and machine learning.
Key goals include helping farmers evaluate trade-offs between different crop rotations, visualize environmental risks, and clearly understand weather uncertainties. Additionally, the challenge encourages participants to apply machine learning to astronaut photography taken from space to extract new insights about land use and agricultural health. By utilizing NASA platforms like Crop-CASMA, OpenET, and satellite datasets from MODIS, VIIRS, and NISAR, innovators can empower growers to adapt their practices, conserve water, and protect crop yields in a rapidly changing climate.
details:
Project name :- AgroShift AI – Precision Crop Adaptation & Risk Simulator.

1. What does it do or how does it work?

AgroShift AI is a web-based decision-support platform that translates complex NASA satellite telemetry into simple, actionable planting and irrigation recommendations for farmers. • Data Ingestion: A user drops a pin on their farm's location. The system automatically fetches historical and near-real-time NASA Earth observation data—including soil moisture (SMAP/Crop-CASMA), evapotranspiration rates (OpenET), surface temperature (ECOSTRESS), and vegetation health (MODIS/VIIRS). • Risk & Trade-off Simulation: Users input their local soil type and current crop rotation. Our machine learning model simulates how different crops will perform over the upcoming season under shifting heat and rainfall scenarios. • Visual Output: The dashboard displays an interactive risk map, highlighting water stress zones and recommending optimal crop alternatives alongside clear probability scores for weather uncertainty.

2. What benefits does it have? • Simplifies Complex Data: Eliminates the need for farmers to understand raw satellite imagery or scientific metrics by converting them into plain-language "Plant / Wait / Switch Crop" insights. • Optimizes Resource Use: Pinpoints exact water deficits, helping growers reduce unnecessary irrigation and fertilizer runoff. • Transparent Uncertainty: Instead of giving a single rigid prediction, the tool visually displays best-case, average, and worst-case yield scenarios so farmers can manage financial risk.

3.What is the intended impact of the project?

Our goal is to empower small-to-medium-scale farmers to adapt proactively to climate volatility rather than reacting to crop failure. By democratizing access to NASA’s Earth science data, AgroShift AI aims to stabilize farm incomes, conserve regional groundwater supplies, and strengthen local food security against prolonged droughts and extreme heatwaves.

4.What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use to develop your project?

• NASA Data & APIs: NASA Earthdata API, OpenET API, Crop-CASMA, AppEEARS (for MODIS and ECOSTRESS subsets), and the Gateway to Astronaut Photography of Earth. • Languages: Python (data processing and ML), JavaScript/TypeScript (frontend), SQL (spatial database queries). • Frameworks & Libraries: React and Mapbox GL JS (interactive geospatial UI), FastAPI (backend), Scikit-Learn & PyTorch (predictive modeling and computer vision), Rasterio & GeoPandas (geospatial data manipulation). • Hardware & Cloud: Developed on standard laptops; deployed using Docker containers on AWS EC2 with PostGIS for spatial data storage.

5. How is your project creative?

• Astronaut Photography Integration: Beyond standard top-down spectral satellites, we trained a lightweight computer vision model on oblique astronaut photography from the ISS to detect regional field boundary shifts and seasonal land-use changes that automated nadir-view algorithms sometimes miss. • "What-If" Gamified Slider: We designed an intuitive climate-stress slider that lets farmers visually watch their fields change color as they simulate a +2°C temperature spike or a 20% drop in seasonal rainfall. 6. Factors Our Team Considered? • Low-Bandwidth Accessibility: Rural farms often have poor internet connectivity. We engineered the backend to compress geospatial tiles and offer a lightweight "SMS/Low-Data Summary Mode." • Actionability Over Raw Metrics: We interviewed agricultural extension workers to ensure we didn't overwhelm users with charts, focusing strictly on metrics tied to immediate farming decisions (planting dates, crop selection, and water budgeting). • Data Latency & Resolution: Satellites have varying revisit times and spatial resolutions. We designed a data-fusion pipeline that blends high-frequency, coarse-resolution data (like SMAP) with less frequent, high-resolution imagery (like Landsat/NISAR) to keep field-level insights accurate.
